Give Those Numbers
A Place to Live

Our random-number app can generate values. Now we want to remember the interesting ones, when they were created, and which system requested them.

From Java object → entity → repository → H2
Spring Boot means springy code. Boing boing. 🌀
DRIVE: JAVA → JPA → H2
DOWN: FIRST
🏈📣🏆⭐🏈
🏈
Save it! Query it! H2 says TOUCHDOWN!
Step 1

Start with an ordinary Java object

The notes begin by calling this concept NotableNumber, then switch to the name MagicNumber for the persisted example. We keep MagicNumber from this point forward so the REST and repository code match.

MagicNumber before persistence
package com.mcnz.random;

import java.time.*;

public class MagicNumber {

    private Instant instant;
    private int randomNumber;

    public MagicNumber(int randomNumber) {
        this.instant = Instant.now();
        this.randomNumber = randomNumber;
    }

    public Instant getInstant() { return instant; }
    public int getRandomNumber() { return randomNumber; }
}
📣

Why do the getters matter here?

When the controller returns the object, Spring's web stack can serialize its visible properties into JSON. The interesting idea is that your Java method returns a Java object while the framework handles the HTTP representation.

Step 2

Turn the class into an entity

The first persistence jump is surprisingly small: identify the class as an entity and give it a primary key that the database can generate.

MagicNumber entity essentials
package com.mcnz.random;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.*;

@Entity
public class MagicNumber {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private Instant instant;
    private int randomNumber;

    public MagicNumber() {}

    public MagicNumber(int randomNumber) {
        this.instant = Instant.now();
        this.randomNumber = randomNumber;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public Instant getInstant() { return instant; }
    public int getRandomNumber() { return randomNumber; }
}
1

@Entity

This class participates in JPA persistence.

2

@Id

This property is the entity's primary key.

3

@GeneratedValue

The database creates the key value for us.

Step 3

Spring Data gives us a repository

By extending CrudRepository<MagicNumber, Long>, the repository already knows how to save, find, and delete MagicNumber entities.

MagicNumberRepository
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.data.repository.*;

public interface MagicNumberRepository
        extends CrudRepository<MagicNumber, Long> {
}
Controller saves the entity
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class NumberController {

    private final RandomNumberService service;
    private final MagicNumberRepository repository;

    public NumberController(
            RandomNumberService service,
            MagicNumberRepository repository) {
        this.service = service;
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @GetMapping("/magic-number")
    public MagicNumber magicNumber() {
        int number = (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * 10) + 1;
        MagicNumber magicNumber = new MagicNumber(number);
        repository.save(magicNumber);
        return magicNumber;
    }
}
⭐

Layering note

For a tiny classroom demo, saving from the controller makes the JPA effect easy to see. In a fuller application, the Module 3 pattern would move persistence orchestration into a service and keep the controller focused on HTTP.

Step 4

Wire H2 with application.properties

Use an in-memory H2 database, let Hibernate create and drop the schema, show generated SQL, and enable the H2 console.

application.properties
spring.application.name=mad-random
server.port=8088
spring.profiles.active=dev

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

spring.h2.console.enabled=true
spring.h2.console.path=/h2-console

REST endpoint

http://localhost:8088/magic-number

If your app uses another port, use that port instead.

H2 console

http://localhost:8088/h2-console/

Use the same JDBC URL configured in your application properties.

⚠️

CHECK YOUR PORT

The supplied notes explicitly warn that your server might be on 8088, 8080, 8085, or another port. The browser URL must match server.port.

Step 5

Add the system that requested the number

Now the model has an association. Many magic numbers can come from one source system, such as a REST server or desktop app.

🔢

MagicNumber

id
instant
randomNumber

* → 1
🖥️

SourceSystem

id
name
detail

SourceSystem
package com.mcnz.random;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
@Table(name = "systems")
public class SourceSystem {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;
    private String detail;

    public SourceSystem() {}

    public SourceSystem(String name, String detail) {
        this.name = name;
        this.detail = detail;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getDetail() { return detail; }
}
Association inside MagicNumber
@ManyToOne(
    fetch = FetchType.EAGER,
    cascade = CascadeType.ALL
)
SourceSystem system;

public SourceSystem getSystem() {
    return system;
}
🗄️

One object graph, multiple inserts

With cascading enabled, persisting the MagicNumber can also persist its associated SourceSystem. Hibernate then generates SQL for both tables and stores the foreign key on the magic-number row.

Step 6

Seed a second source with CommandLineRunner

So far, the REST endpoint represents one way a magic number can enter the system. But your domain model says a number can come from different source systems. Spring Boot's CommandLineRunner gives us a second entry point that is not HTTP at all.

What is CommandLineRunner?

CommandLineRunner is a Spring Boot callback interface. After Spring has created the application context and injected the beans, Spring calls its run(...) method once during startup.

That makes it useful for demo data, initialization work, smoke checks, or one-time startup logic.

Why this is a different system

The earlier web flow can represent a REST Server calling /magic-number. This runner creates another MagicNumber and says its source is Desktop, specifically Windows 11 on a Lenovo Laptop.

Same entity. Same repository. Different entry point and different SourceSystem.

🌐

REST request

SourceSystem: REST Server

→
🗄️

Saves the object graph

Same persistence path

NumberRunner.java
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class NumberRunner implements CommandLineRunner {

    @Autowired
    RandomNumberService service;

    @Autowired
    MagicNumberRepository repository;


    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {

        int number =
            (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * 10);

        MagicNumber magicNumber =
            new MagicNumber(number);

        SourceSystem system =
            new SourceSystem(
                "Desktop",
                "Windows 11 on a Lenovo Laptop"
            );

        magicNumber.system = system;

        repository.save(magicNumber);

        System.out.println(
            "Saved magic number: "
            + magicNumber.getRandomNumber()
        );
    }
}
🏈

Follow the play

1. Spring discovers NumberRunner because it is a @Component. 2. Spring injects RandomNumberService and MagicNumberRepository. 3. After startup, Spring calls run(...). 4. The runner creates a number and a new SourceSystem named Desktop. 5. It attaches that system to the magic number. 6. repository.save(magicNumber) persists the magic number and, because the relationship uses CascadeType.ALL, Hibernate can persist the new source system too.

📣

QUIZ ALERT: one business model, multiple entry points

The important architecture idea is that persistence does not belong only to controllers. A startup runner, REST controller, batch job, or other caller can use the same injected service and repository. That is one of the benefits of keeping HTTP concerns separate from business and persistence concerns.

JPA remembers more than a row

QUIZ ALERT: JPA vs. MyBatis

Later, students are tested on this distinction: JPA entities can be managed by a persistence context and participate in dirty checking. A MyBatis-mapped object is just a POJO after the query returns. Keep this difference in mind as you work with entities here.
